name: Music trivia (medium)
description: 50 medium questions about composers, instruments, genres, famous songs and musicians (no lyrics quoted). Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony sets a text based on an 1785 'Ode to Joy' by which German poet?
items.explain: The finale of the Ninth uses words drawn from Friedrich Schiller's 1785 poem 'Ode to Joy', with a few lines added by Beethoven.

source.title: Symphony No. 9 in D minor, Op. 125 “Choral” (1824)

items.question: In which city was Beethoven's Ninth Symphony first performed, in May 1824?
items.explain: The Ninth Symphony was first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824.

source.title: Beethoven: Ode to Joy - Symphony No. 9, Op. 125

items.question: What groundbreaking element did Beethoven add to the finale of his Ninth Symphony?
items.explain: Beethoven's introduction of vocal soloists and a chorus in the finale was a bold step that expanded what a symphony could do.

source.title: Beethoven, Ludwig van: Symphony No. 9 in D minor, Opus 125, “Choral”

items.question: Vivaldi's The Four Seasons is a set of four concertos for which solo instrument?
items.explain: The Four Seasons is a group of four violin concertos by Antonio Vivaldi, each giving musical expression to a season of the year.

items.question: Vivaldi published The Four Seasons with accompanying poems. It is an early example of which kind of music with a narrative element?
items.explain: Music that tells a story or depicts events is called program music, and The Four Seasons is one of the earliest and most detailed examples.

items.question: The Four Seasons were published in 1725 as the first four concertos in a set of how many?
items.explain: They appeared together with eight more violin concertos, making twelve in the collection 'The Contest Between Harmony and Invention'.

items.question: In which city did the famously scandalous 1913 premiere of Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring take place?
items.explain: The ballet premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris on 29 May 1913.

items.question: For which ballet company did Stravinsky write The Rite of Spring?
items.explain: The piece was commissioned by Serge Diaghilev, impresario of the Ballets Russes, who had also produced Stravinsky's The Firebird and Petrushka.

items.question: Which dancer created the original choreography for The Rite of Spring in 1913?
items.explain: The 1913 production had choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky, with staging and costumes by Nicholas Roerich.

source.title: The riotous premiere of Stravinsky's Rite of Spring

items.question: Which orchestral instrument plays the exposed opening melody of The Rite of Spring?
items.explain: The work is remembered as beginning with a bassoon. Stravinsky openly acknowledged borrowing that melody from a Lithuanian folk song anthology.

source.title: The Premiere of Igor Stravinsky's Rite of Spring

items.question: Which Italian instrument maker is credited with inventing the piano around 1700?
items.explain: Cristofori of Padua, working in Florence, built the first true piano, a hammer-action keyboard instrument, around 1700.

source.title: The Piano: The Pianofortes of Bartolomeo Cristofori (1655–1731) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

items.question: The word 'piano' is short for an early name for an instrument that could play what?
items.explain: Cristofori's instrument was called a 'harpsichord that plays soft and loud'. The name refers to its ability to vary loudness with the pressure on the keys.

items.question: Cristofori developed the first pianos while working for the court of which Italian ruling family?
items.explain: Cristofori was appointed to the Florentine court of Grand Prince Ferdinando de' Medici to care for its harpsichords and other instruments.

source.title: The Piano: The Pianofortes of Bartolomeo Cristofori (1655–1731) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

items.question: Adolphe Sax, the inventor of the saxophone, was a native of which country?
items.explain: Sax was a Belgian inventor and musician, born in Dinant, who later moved to Paris.

items.question: In which year did Adolphe Sax patent the saxophone?
items.explain: Sax patented the saxophone on 28 June 1846, intending it for orchestras and military bands.

items.question: Although saxophones are usually made of brass, to which instrument family do they belong?
items.explain: A saxophone is played with a single-reed mouthpiece like a clarinet's, so it is classed as a woodwind.

source.title: Inspiration and Invention of the Saxophone

items.question: Which early electronic instrument is played without the performer touching it?
items.explain: The theremin is controlled without physical contact: the player moves their hands near two antennas.

items.question: On a theremin, the player's two hands control which two qualities of the sound?
items.explain: One antenna controls pitch and the other controls volume, depending on how close the player's hands are.

items.question: Leon Theremin, inventor of the instrument that bears his name, was a physicist from which country?
items.explain: The instrument was invented around 1920 by the Russian physicist Lev Sergeyevich Termen, known in the West as Leon Theremin.

items.question: Miles Davis's 1959 album Kind of Blue is a landmark recording of which jazz style?
items.explain: Davis based the album entirely on modality. He gave each performer a set of scales to improvise within instead of complex chord changes.

items.question: Which track opens Miles Davis's album Kind of Blue?
items.explain: The album opens with 'So What', a 32-bar tune built on modal simplicity.

source.title: Kind of Blue - Miles Davis's Modal Jazz Masterpiece

items.question: Which pianist was a key figure on Miles Davis's Kind of Blue?
items.explain: Bill Evans is described as a key figure on Kind of Blue, a milepost of jazz history and a leading example of modal jazz.

items.question: In which New York City borough did hip-hop emerge in the early 1970s?
items.explain: Hip-hop's usual birth date is 11 August 1973, at a back-to-school party in the west Bronx where DJ Kool Herc played.

source.title: Hip-hop is born at a teen party in the Bronx

items.question: In which country was DJ Kool Herc, credited as the founder of hip-hop, born?
items.explain: Clive 'Kool Herc' Campbell was born in Kingston, Jamaica, before moving to the Bronx.

items.question: What DJing technique did Kool Herc pioneer at his early Bronx parties?
answers: Slowing records to lower the pitch
items.explain: Herc used two turntables to repeat the 'breakbeat', the percussive section of a record that dancers liked most.

source.title: The South Bronx: Where Hip-Hop Was Born

items.question: Which bandleader commissioned George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue for his 1924 concert 'An Experiment in Modern Music'?
items.explain: Whiteman wanted to elevate American popular music to the level of concert music. He invited Gershwin to compose a jazz concerto for the event.

source.title: Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue Premieres in New York

items.question: Which instrument plays the flamboyant opening solo of Rhapsody in Blue?
items.explain: The piece begins with a famous flamboyant clarinet solo.

items.question: Who suggested the title 'Rhapsody in Blue' to George Gershwin?
items.explain: George Gershwin's brother Ira suggested the new title Rhapsody in Blue while the piece was being prepared for its February 1924 premiere.

source.title: Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue Premieres in New York

items.question: How many movements are in Gustav Holst's orchestral suite The Planets?
items.explain: The Planets is a suite of seven short tone poems, from 'Mars' to 'Neptune'.

items.question: Which of these planets has no movement in Holst's The Planets?
items.explain: The seven movements cover Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Earth is not included.

items.question: Which movement of Holst's The Planets is subtitled 'the Bringer of Jollity'?
items.explain: 'Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity' is the fourth movement and, with 'Mars', one of the most frequently heard.

items.question: Holst's The Planets takes its starting point from which subject?
items.explain: Holst's starting point was the astrological character of each planet, not astronomy or classical mythology.

source.title: The Planets: Suite for large orchestra

items.question: In which city did Handel's Messiah receive its first performance in 1742?
items.explain: Messiah premiered in Dublin on 13 April 1742. London heard it nearly a year later.

items.question: What musical form is Handel's Messiah?
items.explain: Messiah is a large-scale semidramatic work for chorus, soloists and orchestra, and the most frequently performed of all oratorios.

items.question: Who assembled the Biblical verses that Handel set in Messiah?
items.explain: The text was assembled by Handel's friend Charles Jennens, a wealthy supporter of the arts, from several parts of the Bible.

items.question: What does an audience traditionally do when the Hallelujah Chorus is performed?
items.explain: By long tradition, audiences rise to their feet whenever the Hallelujah Chorus is performed.

items.question: In 2016, Bob Dylan became the first musician to win which Nobel Prize?
items.explain: The Swedish Academy honoured Dylan 'for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition'.

source.title: The Nobel Prize in Literature 2016 - Prize announcement - NobelPrize.org

items.question: In which US state was Bob Dylan born?
items.explain: Dylan was born on 24 May 1941 in Duluth, Minnesota.

source.title: Bob Dylan wins 2016 Nobel Prize in literature - ABC30 Fresno

items.question: Which Dylan album did the Swedish Academy's permanent secretary recommend in 2016 as a starting point for newcomers?
items.explain: When Dylan's Nobel win was announced, Sara Danius recommended Blonde on Blonde to those unfamiliar with his work.

source.title: What to Know About Bob Dylan's Nobel Prize for Literature

items.question: Bossa nova blends Brazilian samba with which other musical style?
items.explain: Bossa nova is a blend of Brazilian samba and jazz, and 'The Girl from Ipanema' helped popularize it worldwide.

items.question: Which Brazilian guitarist is widely known as the 'father of bossa nova'?
items.explain: João Gilberto is called the Father of Bossa Nova for the guitar style he developed from traditional samba.

source.title: Remembering the "Father of Bossa Nova" João Gilberto (RIP) with Four Classic Live Performances: “The Girl From Ipanema,” "Corcovado” & More

items.question: Who composed the music of 'The Girl from Ipanema'?
items.explain: The song was co-written by the poet Vinícius de Moraes and the composer Antônio Carlos Jobim.

items.question: Which American saxophonist played on the 1964 hit recording of 'The Girl from Ipanema'?
items.explain: The recording became the biggest hit of Stan Getz's career, with Astrud Gilberto adding English vocals.

items.question: Which French composer wrote the opera Carmen, which premiered in Paris in 1875?
items.explain: Carmen is an opera by Georges Bizet that premiered in Paris on 3 March 1875.

items.question: Bizet's Carmen is set in Spain. In which language is it sung?
items.explain: Despite its Spanish setting, Carmen is sung in French, as Bizet was a French composer writing for Paris.

items.question: Which character sings the famous 'Toreador Song' in Bizet's Carmen?
items.explain: The 'Toreador Song' is Escamillo's showpiece. Along with Carmen's 'Habanera', it is among the opera's best-known music.

source.title: Bizet’s Carmen: Songs, Synopsis, Plot & More

items.question: What is the title character's job at the start of Bizet's Carmen?
items.explain: Carmen is a fiery cigarette factory worker whose relationship with the soldier Don José drives the story.

items.question: Which ballet was Tchaikovsky's first, composed in 1876?
items.explain: Swan Lake (1876) came before The Sleeping Beauty (1889) and The Nutcracker (1892). The Sleeping Beauty was Tchaikovsky's second ballet.

items.question: Which choreographer collaborated with Tchaikovsky on the celebrated 1890 production of The Sleeping Beauty?
items.explain: The 1890 Sleeping Beauty was Tchaikovsky's first collaboration with the choreographer Marius Petipa.

source.title: Tchaikovsky’s Ballets: Swan Lake, Sleeping Beauty, Nutcracker

items.question: The Sleeping Beauty (1890) and The Nutcracker (1892) both premiered on the stage of which theatre?
items.explain: Both ballets were commissioned by the Russian Imperial Theatres and premiered on the Mariinsky stage in St. Petersburg.

source.title: Classical Net Review - Tchaikovsky - Swan Lake/Sleeping Beauty/Nutcracker
